Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown has branded the cholera crisis in Zimbabwe "an international emergency" and called on the world community to confront President Robert Mugabe, leader of the central African nation. A shortage of clean drinking water has unleashed a cholera epidemic in Zimbabwe. "This is now an international rather than a national emergency," Brown said in a statement Saturday. "International because disease crosses borders. International because the systems of government in Zimbabwe are now broken. There is no state capable or willing of protecting its people." Earlier this week the government of Zimbabwe, which already suffers from severe economic problems and political instability, declared a national emergency following the outbreak, which has so far killed more than 600 people. Cholera, a water-borne disease, is on the increase in nine of Zimbabwe's 10 provinces, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned. It blamed "poor water and sanitation supply, a collapsed health system and limited government capacity to respond to the emergency." Many of those afflicted with the disease have fled to neighboring countries to seek medical help -- which risks spreading the outbreak still further. Brown called on the international community to tell Mugabe "enough is enough," and suggested that the United Nations Security Council meet to discuss the issue. He added that the most pressing issue was to ensure that testing and rehydration equipment and packs reach the right people, as well as for aid agencies to set up a organizational structure in the state capital Harare to confront the disease. "The people of Zimbabwe voted for a better future. It is our duty to support that aspiration," Brown added.   Brown's comments came one day after U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said that the outbreak is the latest sign that Mugabe's rule over the country must end. "It's well past time for Robert Mugabe to leave. I think that's now obvious," Rice said during a visit to Denmark. Washington has long called for Mugabe to leave office, with President George W. Bush calling Zimbabwe's runoff presidential election in June a "sham" and instructing Rice and other U.S. officials to develop additional sanctions against Mugabe's "illegitimate government." "The United States will always do anything and everything that it can to help innocent people who are suffering," Rice said. "And we are not going to deny assistance to people in need because of their government. But if this is not evidence to the international community that it's time to stand up for what is right, I don't know what will be. And frankly, the nations of the region have to lead it." Rice -- who has just about a month left in office before President-elect Barack Obama's administration takes over -- also called on all African nations to speak up. Asked whether the United States and Europe should try to force out Mugabe, Rice responded, "Well, without help in the region, it's very difficult to have the tools that will bring about a just resolution in Zimbabwe. The United States and Europe can't do everything alone. Other states are responsible too. And the southern African states should be the most responsible at this point, because they have the most at risk. And the people of Zimbabwe have suffered long enough." Supporters of Mugabe, who has come under heavy international criticism for several years, were accused of political intimidation following June's presidential  runoff vote. For months there have been some efforts to build a power-sharing government between Mugabe's ruling Zanu PF party and the opposition movement for Democratic Change, led by Morgan Tsvangirai, to little avail. On Thursday, Mugabe hinted he may form a Cabinet without the opposition and call for early elections. The opposition responded that it would welcome a "genuine election," with international supervision. The 84-year-old Mugabe, who has led Zimbabwe since its independence in 1980 from Great Britain, also suggested he would ignore an international tribunal ruling that declared illegal his government's seizure of farms from white Zimbabweans.

The rapid spread of the preventable waterborne disease has highlighted the extreme severity of the humanitarian crisis currently gripping the nation.

**Headline:** A State in Collapse: Global Calls for Action Grow as Zimbabwe’s Cholera Epidemic Threatens Regional Stability

**HARARE / LONDON** — What began as a preventable public health challenge has deteriorated into a devastating humanitarian and political catastrophe in Zimbabwe. As a severe cholera epidemic tears through the country’s provinces and spills across international borders, the crisis has exposed the total breakdown of the nation’s infrastructure under the rule of President Robert Mugabe. In response, British Prime Minister Gordon Brown has issued a sharp condemnation of the regime, calling for immediate international intervention, emergency aid deployment, and decisive action by the United Nations Security Council to address what he termed a failed state.

The outbreak, which has already claimed more than 600 lives and infected thousands more, is a direct consequence of Zimbabwe’s crumbling municipal services. Decades of economic mismanagement, hyperinflation, and political corruption have left the capital of Harare and surrounding urban centers without basic sanitation, clean drinking water, or functioning sewage systems. Deprived of chemical treatment agents, municipal water supplies have become vectors for the waterborne disease. Compounding the tragedy, the national healthcare system has virtually collapsed; hospitals lack essential medicines, and doctors and nurses have been forced to strike after hyperinflation rendered their wages worthless.

The crisis is no longer contained within Zimbabwe's borders. As thousands of desperate citizens flee the economic and sanitary disaster, cholera cases have been reported in neighboring South Africa, Botswana, and Mozambique. In the South African border town of Musina, health clinics are struggling to process a continuous influx of infected refugees, raising fears of a broader, uncontrollable regional epidemic that could destabilize Southern Africa.

Speaking from London, Prime Minister Gordon Brown described the situation as a moral outrage and a clear signal of the regime’s complete failure to protect its people. Declaring that "enough is enough," Brown urged the international community to bypass the political deadlock in Harare and take urgent action. He called on the UN Security Council to formally convene, coordinate a massive emergency medical relief effort, and directly challenge the legitimacy of Mugabe’s government. 

For years, the Mugabe regime has attributed the nation's severe economic decline to foreign sanctions. However, international observers and human rights organizations view the cholera outbreak as the ultimate proof of man-made state failure. Rather than mobilizing national resources to contain the disease, the government in Harare initially denied the severity of the crisis and attempted to suppress information regarding the death toll.

The rapidly mounting casualties demonstrate that the humanitarian crisis cannot be separated from the political one. Public health experts and international leaders agree that delivering intravenous fluids and water purification tablets is only a temporary fix. To permanently end the suffering of the Zimbabwean people and avert a widening regional disaster, the international community must confront the root cause of the tragedy: the end of Robert Mugabe’s oppressive regime and a swift transition toward legitimate, accountable governance.

**'Enough is enough': World leaders demand Mugabe step down as Zimbabwe cholera crisis deepens**

December 7, 2008 
From CNN International

**(CNN)** -- A catastrophic cholera outbreak in Zimbabwe has sparked a fresh wave of international fury, with top Western officials declaring "enough is enough" and calling for the immediate end of President Robert Mugabe’s nearly three-decade rule.

With the country's health and sanitation systems in total collapse, the United Nations reports that the preventable waterborne disease has killed more than 500 people, with suspected cases topping 12,000. 

As the death toll climbs daily, British Prime Minister Gordon Brown launched a scathing attack on the Mugabe regime on Sunday, describing the humanitarian disaster as an "international emergency."

"Mugabe's regime has failed," Brown said in a statement. "The economic collapse, the health collapse, the refusal to recognize the result of an election... enough is enough. A blood-stained regime with a tragic record of failure is facing a catastrophe."

Brown urged the international community to unite in telling Mugabe to step aside, adding that he was in talks with African leaders to coordinate a stronger response to the rapidly worsening situation.

**'Past time for Mugabe to go'**

The British Prime Minister's sharp rebuke follows similar comments from U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who said last week that the stalled political process and the deepening humanitarian crisis proved Mugabe had lost all legitimacy.

Speaking to reporters during a visit to Copenhagen, Denmark, Rice blamed Mugabe’s refusal to share power with the political opposition following disputed elections earlier this year.

"If this does not show to the international community that it is time for Robert Mugabe to go, then I don't know what will," Rice said. "It's well past time for Robert Mugabe to go."

Rice noted that the power-sharing negotiations—brokered by South Africa—had become a "sham" due to Mugabe’s unwillingness to cede control over key security agencies to Opposition Leader Morgan Tsvangirai of the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC).

**Hospitals overwhelmed, water turned off**

In the capital city of Harare, the situation on the ground is grim. Thousands of people lack access to safe drinking water after the state-run water authority ran out of foreign currency to purchase essential water treatment chemicals. 

Untreated sewage now flows freely through streets in densely populated townships like Budiriro and Chitungwiza, the epicenters of the outbreak.

The country's public healthcare system has essentially ceased to function. Major hospitals in Harare have shut down their doors because doctors and nurses, whose salaries have been rendered worthless by hyperinflation estimated in the quintillions of percent, simply cannot afford the bus fare to report to work. 

"People are dying at the gates of hospitals," said a medical worker in Harare, speaking to CNN on the condition of anonymity out of fear of government reprisal. "We have no rehydration fluids, no gloves, no medicines. It is not that we cannot treat cholera—cholera is easy to treat—it is that we have nothing left to treat it with."

Last week, the Zimbabwean government officially declared a national health emergency and solicited international aid, a rare admission of crisis from Harare. 

**Regime blames Western sanctions**

Despite the mounting international pressure, Mugabe’s government has pushed back fiercely against calls for his resignation. 

State-run media in Zimbabwe accused the United Kingdom and the United States of using the cholera outbreak as a pretext for "regime change" and military intervention. Government spokesman Bright Matonga rejected Brown and Rice's comments, blaming Western-imposed economic sanctions for the country's collapse.

"Gordon Brown is dreaming," Matonga told reporters in Harare. "The sanctions imposed by Britain and America are what have crippled our health system, not President Mugabe."

However, relief agencies and human rights groups dismiss the government's claims, pointing out that Western sanctions specifically target individuals in Mugabe's inner circle and state-owned companies tied to human rights abuses, not humanitarian or medical supplies.

As aid agencies rush water purification tablets and medical supplies to the region, diplomats say the United Nations Security Council is expected to hold informal discussions on the crisis in the coming days. But with neighboring South Africa still favoring a diplomatic solution through the Southern African Development Community (SADC), it remains unclear whether the international community can forge a consensus to force Mugabe from power.

For ordinary Zimbabweans, political maneuvering offers little immediate comfort.

"We are hungry, we have no money, and now the water we drink is killing us," said a resident of Harare. "We just want to survive."

*CNN's David McKenzie and diplomatic correspondents contributed to this report.*

The humanitarian catastrophe, combined with a months-long political paralyzation following a blood-soaked presidential election, has pushed the international community to a breaking point. Over the weekend, top Western diplomats abandoned diplomatic ambiguity, openly calling for the resignation of 84-year-old President Robert Mugabe.

In London, British Prime Minister Gordon Brown issued an unprecedentedly sharp rebuke, characterizing Mugabe’s government as a threat to global conscience. 

"A rogue regime has inflicted a cholera epidemic, land seizures, and hyperinflation on a once-vibrant nation," Brown said in a statement. "The international community’s message must be simple and unyielding: enough is enough. Mugabe’s regime is a failed state, and it is time for him to go."

Brown urged the United Nations Security Council to convene urgently to address the crisis, calling on regional powers to withdraw their tacit support for the veteran ruler.

Echoing the British Prime Minister, US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice delivered a damning assessment during a visit to Copenhagen. 

"The departure of Robert Mugabe is long overdue," Rice stated firmly. "The elections in Zimbabwe were a sham. The power-sharing negotiations have been dragged out while the humanitarian situation deteriorates daily. It is time for the international community to stand up and say to Mugabe that it is time to step down."

The current disaster is the culmination of a political crisis that ignited in March, when opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai and his Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) defeated Mugabe and the ruling ZANU-PF party in the first round of the presidential election. However, before a required runoff could be held in June, the regime launched a brutal campaign of state-sponsored violence. MDC offices were raided, and more than 100 opposition supporters were murdered, while thousands were tortured. 

Citing the impossibility of a free and fair vote, Tsvangirai withdrew from the June election. Mugabe proceeded with a one-man runoff, declaring himself the victor in a ballot widely condemned as illegal by international observers and regional bodies alike. 

Though former South African President Thabo Mbeki brokered a fragile power-sharing agreement in September, implementation has stalled completely. Mugabe has refused to yield control over key security ministries, prompting Tsvangirai to refuse to enter a government where his party would be powerless to stop ongoing human rights abuses.

"We cannot be junior partners in an administration that continues to oppress our people," Tsvangirai said in an interview in Harare this week. "The people voted for change, not for a continuation of the ZANU-PF dictatorship."

While the political impasse drags on in air-conditioned conference rooms, ordinary Zimbabweans are paying a lethal price. The roots of the country's economic and infrastructural collapse trace back nearly a decade to Mugabe’s controversial land reform program. 

Beginning in 2000, the regime orchestrated the violent seizure of thousands of white-owned commercial farms. Ostensibly meant to redress colonial-era imbalances, the land was largely handed to political loyalists and ZANU-PF cronies with little agricultural experience. The policy decimated Zimbabwe’s primary export sector, triggering hyperinflation currently estimated in the hundreds of millions of percent. 

Without foreign currency, municipalities lost the ability to purchase imported water purification chemicals like aluminum sulfate. In Harare, water taps ran dry months ago. Residents turned to digging shallow wells near leaking pit latrines, creating the ideal breeding ground for *Vibrio cholerae*. 

Hospitals, once the envy of Africa, have effectively shut down. Doctors and nurses, their monthly salaries rendered worthless by hyperinflation—often insufficient to cover a single day's bus fare—have gone on strike. Basic medical supplies, from intravenous drips to oral rehydration salts, are virtually non-existent.

In response to the mounting Western pressure, Mugabe’s government remains defiant. Information Minister Sikhanyiso Ndlovu dismissed the foreign criticism today, accusing Western powers of using the cholera outbreak as a pretext to overthrow the government. Ndlovu went so far as to label the epidemic a "biological weapon" introduced by Britain.

Yet, on the ground, the reality cannot be spun away. At the South African border post of Beitbridge, thousands of sick and starving Zimbabweans are wading across the Limpopo River daily, seeking medical treatment and asylum in neighboring countries, threatening to destabilize the entire region.

For the citizens of Harare, the lofty statements from London and Washington offer little immediate relief. As rain begins to fall across the city—threatening to spread the waterborne bacteria even further—the national mood is one of quiet, agonizing desperation.

"We survived the political violence in June," said a schoolteacher in Highfield, holding a handkerchief over her face as she walked past a pool of stagnant water. "Now we are just trying to survive our own drinking water. We have no leaders left to save us."

**HARARE, Zimbabwe** — Zimbabwe has plunged into an unprecedented national emergency as a catastrophic cholera outbreak and a spiraling political stalemate threaten to completely collapse the nation’s basic infrastructure. 

With public hospitals shuttered, municipal water systems failing, and the economy crushed by hyperinflation, international aid agencies are warning of a humanitarian disaster of terrifying proportions, prompting sharp condemnation and calls for political change from major world powers.

### U.N. OCHA Warns of a Deteriorating Catastrophe

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) issued a stark warning this week, declaring that Zimbabwe's public health system has effectively collapsed. According to OCHA, the cholera epidemic—spread primarily through contaminated drinking water—has already claimed hundreds of lives, with tens of thousands of suspected cases reported across the country. 

"The combination of uncollected garbage, broken sewage pipes, and a total lack of water treatment chemicals has turned Harare and surrounding townships into breeding grounds for disease," OCHA stated in a emergency briefing. The U.N. agency warned that without immediate, large-scale international intervention, the death toll could rise exponentially, noting that severe shortages of basic medical supplies, clean water, and qualified medical staff—many of whom are on strike over unpaid wages—have left clinics unable to treat the sick.

OCHA emphasized that the health crisis is compounded by severe food insecurity, leaving millions of malnourished citizens exceptionally vulnerable to the waterborne disease.

### Refugee Exodus Overwhelms Neighboring States

Desperate to escape both the deadly outbreak and the country's economic ruin, thousands of Zimbabweans are fleeing daily across the nation’s borders. 

The crisis is rapidly spilling into neighboring countries. At the border town of Musina, South Africa, authorities report being overwhelmed by an influx of thousands of refugees crossing the Limpopo River. Health officials in South Africa’s Limpopo province have declared the border zone a disaster area after dozens of arriving refugees tested positive for cholera, threatening a wider regional epidemic. 

Refugee processing centers in South Africa and Botswana are operating far beyond capacity. Humanitarian workers on the ground describe dire scenes of exhausted families sleeping in open fields, lacking shelter, sanitation, and food. Human rights groups report that many refugees are risking hazardous wild crossings and exploitation by smugglers simply to gain access to basic healthcare and clean water denied to them at home.

### International Outcry: Demands from Washington and London

The dual health and political crises have intensified international pressure on President Robert Mugabe, whose regime remains locked in a bitter political stalemate with the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), led by Morgan Tsvangirai, following contested and violent elections earlier this year.

In London, British Prime Minister Gordon Brown launched a scathing attack on Mugabe’s administration, calling the situation a "stand-still tragedy" and declaring that the international community must say "enough is enough."

"The people of Zimbabwe are suffering needlessly," Brown said in an official statement from Downing Street. "A failed state is collapsing before our eyes, bringing disease and devastation to its people. The Mugabe regime has lost all legitimacy and can no longer fulfill the most basic duties of government. We are working closely with international partners to demand urgent action at the United Nations."

In Washington, the U.S. State Department echoed London's outrage, placing the blame for the humanitarian disaster squarely on Mugabe’s refusal to yield power. 

U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice stated that power-sharing negotiations had become a "farce" used by the regime to cling to control. "It is long past time for Robert Mugabe to step aside," Rice declared during a press briefing in Washington. "The election was stolen, the economy is destroyed, and now the regime's incompetence is literally killing its own citizens through a preventable disease outbreak. Washington stands ready to support a democratic Zimbabwe, but Mugabe’s continued rule is an obstacle to the survival of his people."

U.S. President George W. Bush also issued a statement urging regional leaders, particularly the Southern African Development Community (SADC), to exert real pressure on Harare to end the political blockade and allow unhindered access for international aid agencies.

### A Regime in Denial

Despite the mounting body count and international isolation, the Zimbabwean government has rejected blame. State media and government spokespersons in Harare have dismissed the international outcry as Western propaganda, claiming the cholera outbreak is under control and accusing Western nations of using the health crisis as a pretext to force regime change.

However, on the ground in Harare, the reality is inescapable. Outside overcrowded treatment centers managed by Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) and the U.N., long lines of sick citizens wait under the scorching sun, serving as a grim testament to a nation sliding deeper into disaster.
